<span id="top"></span>

A **vision foundation model** is a large image encoder pretrained on broad image collections so that its internal features can be reused for many later tasks. Vision Transformers divide an image into patches, treat those patches as tokens and learn relationships among them. Self-supervised models such as DINO learn useful visual structure without requiring a class label for every pretraining image.

In these projects, students do not train a foundation model from the beginning. They start from a pretrained backbone and add only what is needed for the task — often nothing at all, because DINO's patch features are already strong enough to compare images directly. For industrial inspection, patch-level representations may show where a surface differs from normal examples.

The central evaluation separates what the pretrained backbone already provides from what the student's adaptation contributes. A frozen backbone, a parameter-efficient adapter and — where hardware permits — a full fine-tune are compared using the same data, split and backbone, with performance reported alongside the number of trainable parameters and the compute cost.

::: {.category-callout}
**Three ways to adapt a pretrained backbone**

**Freeze it** and compare features directly, or train only a small head. **Adapt it efficiently** by inserting small trainable modules (LoRA or adapters) into an otherwise frozen network, typically training under 10% of the parameters. **Fine-tune everything**, which is the most expressive and the most expensive. Knowing how much each step actually buys is the point of these projects.
:::

## Learn first and find ideas

- Core reading: [DINO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14294), [DINOv2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07193), the [DINOv2 model card and code](https://github.com/facebookresearch/dinov2), and [AnomalyDINO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14529).
- Parameter-efficient adaptation: [LoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685) and the [Hugging Face PEFT library](https://github.com/huggingface/peft).
- Data and model hubs: [MVTec AD](https://www.mvtec.com/research-teaching/datasets/mvtec-ad), [Hugging Face models](https://huggingface.co/models) and [timm](https://github.com/huggingface/pytorch-image-models).
- Keep zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot and full-shot anomaly results separate, and never compare an image-level metric directly with a pixel-level metric.

## 3.1  Adapting DINO backbones for industrial anomaly detection {#project-3-1}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localisation</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">BSc or MSc</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Light for the frozen route (no training); moderate for adapters — a single 8–16 GB consumer GPU covers the whole project</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">[MVTec AD](https://www.mvtec.com/research-teaching/datasets/mvtec-ad) — 5,354 images, 15 categories, pixel-precise masks, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">Oquab et al., [DINOv2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07193), 2023</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** A DINOv2 backbone produces strong general-purpose image features without ever having seen an industrial defect. Find out how much of the work is already done by those frozen features, and how much is added by actually adapting the backbone to the inspection task.
:::

**Data.** MVTec AD is the standard benchmark that comparable published work reports on, which makes results directly comparable. Most categories contain only 60–390 defect-free training images, so this is a one-class problem. [MVTec AD 2](https://www.mvtec.com/company/research/datasets/mvtec-ad-2) (8,000+ images, 8 harder scenarios) is the MSc secondary benchmark — see the Master scope for why it matters. Both are non-commercial research licences.

**Methods and code.** DINOv2 **ViT-S/14** by default, or ViT-B/14 with ≥16 GB, from the [official Apache-2.0 repository](https://github.com/facebookresearch/dinov2). The frozen route follows [AnomalyDINO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14529)'s patch-similarity approach, which is **training-free** — only a forward pass. Parameter-efficient adaptation uses LoRA or adapter modules via [PEFT](https://github.com/huggingface/peft). Do not use ViT-L/g or DINOv3 ViT-7B; they are unnecessary here and outside the compute budget.

**Baselines and evaluation.** Frozen DINOv2 with patch nearest-neighbour scoring; a frozen linear or MLP probe; LoRA or adapter adaptation; full fine-tuning only if hardware permits; and a non-DINO reference such as PatchCore-style nearest neighbours over an ImageNet-pretrained CNN. Report image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and PRO per category, **and** the number of trainable parameters plus GPU memory and training time for each condition — the cost side is part of the result, not an afterthought.

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Bachelor research question.** **How much of DINOv2's anomaly-detection performance is already present in its frozen features, before any training?**

*Core experiment.* Compare three conditions on MVTec AD with ViT-S/14: frozen features with patch nearest-neighbour scoring (no training at all), a frozen linear probe, and one LoRA configuration. Report accuracy against trainable-parameter count for each.

The frozen baseline requires no training, so a working anomaly detector is available from the start and the project time goes into analysis.
:::

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master research question.** **How much can parameter-efficient adaptation recover of the gap between frozen features and full fine-tuning, at a fraction of the trainable parameters — and does that trade-off change on a benchmark that has not yet saturated?** Run the full ladder — frozen, linear probe, LoRA/adapter, full fine-tune — on **both** MVTec AD and MVTec AD 2, with parameter counts and compute cost reported throughout.

**Why the second benchmark.** MVTec AD is saturated: published methods cluster above 99% image AUROC, so all four adaptation strategies may look identical on it. MVTec AD 2 was built in response to that saturation and current methods score below 60% AU-PRO, leaving room for the comparison to resolve a difference. An optional extension is continued self-supervised pretraining on the target domain before adaptation, following [ExPLoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05493).
:::

**Practical notes.** DINOv2 is ungated and Apache 2.0 — build the pipeline on it first. MVTec's licence is non-commercial, so results cannot be repurposed for industrial use without separate permission.
